body_en:
Original paper: PDF (GitHub Release) | Official link (DOI), published in Gastroenterology, 2019.

Led by Peking University Health Science Center and Renji Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, together with 308 hospitals across China, this study spent three years collecting 25,927 confirmed cases — the largest registry of drug-induced liver injury ever assembled in China. Every number below comes from it.

Many people take herbal medicine because it feels “natural” and “side-effect-free.” But this nationwide study — 308 hospitals, three years, 25,927 cases — says the opposite: in China, traditional Chinese medicine and herbal supplements are the number-one cause of drug-induced liver injury.

Drug-Induced Liver Injury Is Worse in China Than in the West

The study covered hospital admissions from 2012 to 2014. In the 66 hospitals with complete reporting used to estimate incidence, 8.1 million inpatients were admitted over three years, and 13,691 cases of drug-induced liver injury were identified. The findings:

  • China's annual incidence of drug-induced liver injury is estimated at 23.8 cases per 100,000 people — higher than France (13.9), Iceland (19.1), the United States (2.7), Spain (3.42), and Sweden (2.4).
  • Among inpatients, 1.69 out of every 100 had drug-induced liver injury.
  • And even that is an underestimate: the study only counted hospital admissions. Mild cases handled as outpatients weren't included, and coverage in less developed regions was incomplete — the true incidence can only be higher.

The Leading Culprit: Herbal Medicine and Dietary Supplements

Among all cases, the leading causes were:

  • Traditional Chinese medicine, herbal remedies, and dietary supplements: 26.81%, ranked first
  • Anti-tuberculosis drugs: 21.99%, ranked second
  • Antitumor and immunomodulatory drugs: 8.34%, ranked third

That 26.81% isn't a rough guess. Every case in the study was scored with the RUCAM causality assessment; cases that weren't clear-cut were reviewed one by one by a panel of three hepatologists, and only counted when at least two agreed it was “highly probable.” More than one in four cases of drug-induced liver injury was caused by herbal medicine and dietary supplements. The study also names specific culprits with confirmed liver toxicity: He Shou Wu (Polygonum multiflorum), Lei Gong Teng (Tripterygium wilfordii), and Xiao Chai Hu Tang (Minor Bupleurum decoction). Laboratory studies confirm these trigger immune activation, metabolic disruption, and liver cell death.

Worse still, herbal medicine tends to damage the liver after a longer delay than Western drugs — symptoms can appear long after you start taking it, so many people never connect the two.

How Bad Is the Damage?

These numbers come from 25,927 confirmed cases — not a small sample of a few dozen:

  • Over half (51.39%) had hepatocellular injury, and 44.40% of those met “Hy's Law” criteria — a marker in drug-induced liver injury that signals a potentially fatal course.
  • 13% progressed to chronic liver injury, with liver function still abnormal after six months.
  • 280 people (1.08%) developed liver failure; 2 received liver transplants; 102 died (0.39%). Of the 102 deaths, 72 were caused by the liver injury itself.
  • Women and older patients suffered more severe damage; herbal-induced liver injury was also more common in women.

One easily overlooked point: 80.76% of cases had no jaundice. In other words, most liver injury is invisible from the outside — by the time it's noticed, it may already be serious.

Why Herbal Medicine Became the Number-One Culprit

The study puts it bluntly: many Chinese people take herbal medicine based on a mistaken belief — that it's “basically harmless.” Add weak regulation of herbal production and sales, and misuse becomes easy. People take herbs with known liver toxicity, like He Shou Wu and Lei Gong Teng, without any idea of the risk.

“Natural” is not the same as “safe.” Herbal medicine is still medicine, and all medicine has toxicity — it's just that the toxicity is often hidden behind the words “traditional” and “natural.”

Taking Herbal Medicine? Watch for These

  • If you develop fatigue, poor appetite, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes while taking herbal medicine, get your liver function checked promptly.
  • No jaundice doesn't mean your liver is fine — regular liver function tests are more reliable than waiting for symptoms.
  • Tell your doctor about every herbal medicine and supplement you take; don't leave them out because “herbal medicine doesn't count as medicine.”
  • People with existing liver disease need extra caution: 23.38% of cases in the study already had liver disease, and among the deaths, that figure reached 64.32%.

One Caveat

In this study, “traditional Chinese medicine” is a broad category covering Chinese herbal medicine, Tibetan and Mongolian medicine, health products, and dietary supplements — the 26.81% figure is for that whole category combined. The inclusion criteria were also relatively broad, with mild cases counted, so the mortality rate (0.39%) looks lower than in some Western registries. But that doesn't change the conclusion: incidence is higher, and the leading cause is herbal medicine. Both points stand.

Source: 308 hospitals nationwide, 25,927 confirmed cases, published in Gastroenterology, 2019. Links to the original paper (PDF and official link) are at the top of this article.
excerpt_en: A landmark study of 25,927 patients across 308 hospitals found traditional Chinese medicine and herbal supplements are the single biggest cause of drug-induced liver injury in China — far ahead of any Western drug class.
title_en: Herbal Medicine and Liver Damage: China's Leading Cause of Drug-Induced Liver Injury
